title: Modi Doubles Down on 'Dimagi Naxal' Rhetoric at Delhi College Centenary
excerpt: Addressing students at SRCC's 100th anniversary, the prime minister compared his controversial phrase to a homeopathic remedy that forces critics to reveal themselves.
body:
• PM Modi addressed the centenary celebrations of Shri Ram College of Commerce (SRCC) in Delhi on Saturday, reprising his 'dimagi Naxal' label from his Independence Day speech.
  • He compared the phrase to a homeopathic pill that makes an illness worse before curing it, arguing critics revealed their 'true colours' by reacting to the term.
  • The speech combined political attacks on the opposition with appeals to Gen Z to contribute to India's development goals.
  • The address comes weeks after youth-led protests forced the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over examination irregularities.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi used the centenary celebrations of Shri Ram College of Commerce in New Delhi on Saturday to amplify his recently coined 'dimagi Naxal' label, turning a university event into a platform for both political messaging and youth outreach.

Modi first deployed the phrase during his Independence Day address from the Red Fort on August 15, declaring that while armed Naxalism was 'breathing its last' after years of security operations, India now faced a threat from 'dimagi Naxals' — people who align with the Maoist movement's ideology without taking up arms.

The Homeopathic Analogy

At SRCC, Modi offered an extended metaphor to defend the phrase. He compared 'dimagi Naxal' to a homeopathic remedy that temporarily aggravates symptoms before providing a cure.

https://x.com/narendramodi/status/2096259811130351872

"As soon as I gave the 'dimagi Naxal' homeopathic pill, all the mental Naxals started coming out one after another. And now the public is also seeing the true colours of those who are promoting this illness."

— PM Narendra Modi, at SRCC centenary

The remark drew cheers from students and faculty. Modi used the reaction to argue that his critics had inadvertently validated the label by objecting to it publicly.

Political Context

The speech arrives against significant political headwinds. A 36-day student agitation over NEET examination irregularities and paper-leak scandals put the BJP-led government under sustained pressure this summer, culminating in the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. The Cockroach Janta Party, a youth-led protest movement, emerged as a rare challenge to Modi's government during the unrest.

Modi did not address the protests directly. Instead, he highlighted his government's economic record, asserting that India had grown from a 'fragile' economy into the world's fastest-growing major economy with a 7.8 percent quarterly growth rate. He contrasted his administration's handling of successive crises — the COVID-19 pandemic, the Russia-Ukraine war, global trade disruptions — with what he described as inadequate crisis management by the previous government during the 2008 financial crisis and the 2013 Kedarnath disaster.

Opposition Pushback

The 'dimagi Naxal' label has drawn sharp responses from opposition figures since Modi first used it at the Red Fort. Union Minister Kiren Rijiju subsequently published a list of individuals he associated with the term, prompting former Finance Minister P. Chidambaram to respond that he was 'proud to be one.'

CPI General Secretary D. Raja accused Modi of adding another label to a catalogue of right-wing tropes used to suppress dissent. Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra sarcastically embraced the term, posting: 'I am a dimaagi Naxal. All cockroaches by definition are.'

Cockroach Janta Party spokesperson Saurav Das rejected what he called a loose branding of educated young people as Naxals for questioning the government.

Youth Outreach

Modi had previously visited SRCC in 2013 as Gujarat chief minister, an appearance that drew considerable social media attention ahead of the 2014 general election. His return visit combined the political combativeness with appeals to Gen Z ambition, urging students to think beyond immediate challenges and contribute to building what his government calls a 'Viksit Bharat' — a developed India by 2047.

The dual messaging — attacking opponents while courting young voters — reflects the BJP's broader strategic recalibration following the student protest movement that challenged its hold on the youth constituency.
